pl-l3d15c3-d1e114.summary: Gives the chapter's subject: obscure chapters of Hilary in which the pains of the passion seem to be removed from Christ's flesh.

pl-l3d15c3-d1e117.summary: States the difficulty: Hilary's words are more troubling, seeming to teach that blows and wounds so fell on Christ as not to cause pain, as a weapon passing through water, fire, or air does what it does in a living body, piercing and pricking, but causes no pain, since those things cannot feel. So, he says, Christ's body received the force of punishment without its sense, since as our body cannot walk on water, so Christ's body did not have the nature of our pain.
claims: Hilary seems to say Christ's body received the force of punishment without pain.

pl-l3d15c3-d1e120.summary: Quotes Hilary, De Trinitate X: the only God took true man like ours without ceasing to be God; though blows fell, wounds came, knots bound, and suspension raised him, these brought the force of suffering but not its pain, like a weapon piercing water, pricking fire, or wounding air. Christ suffered when struck, hung, and died, but the passion did not exercise its nature; the strength of his body received the force of punishment without its sense. His body had the nature of our pain only if our body can walk on waves and pass through closed doors; that flesh is from heaven, that man from God, having a body to suffer, and he suffered, but not having a nature to feel pain.
claims: Christ suffered but did not have a nature to feel pain, according to Hilary.
Christ's body had powers ours lacks.

pl-l3d15c3-d1e132.summary: Continues Hilary: let us see if the order of the passion lets us understand weakness of pain in the Lord. Fear cannot be signified in his words when his confidence appears in his deeds. Did he fear who went out to meet armed men, before whom the crowds fell backward? Did he fear the pain of nails who restored a severed ear by a touch? Could the hand that restored an ear feel the nail?
claims: Christ's deeds show he did not fear the passion, according to Hilary.

pl-l3d15c3-d1e139.summary: Concludes Hilary: comparing the power of words and deeds, it is clear that the weakness of bodily nature was not in his body, and the passion, though inflicted on the body, did not bring it the nature of pain; though our bodily form was in the Lord, the form of our vicious weakness was not in the body the Virgin bore from the Spirit's conception.
claims: The weakness of our vicious nature was not in Christ's body.

pl-l3d15c3-d1e145.summary: Interprets Hilary: the attentive reader who looks at the context can grasp his meaning and will not attack it. He says the pain of the passion did not fall on Christ, and his body received the force of punishment without its sense, because he did not have in himself the cause and merit of pain, as he marks in 'not having a nature to feel pain'. So his flesh is not to be judged by the nature of our body, and passion had no dominion over him; likewise he had no nature to fear or grieve, since he had no nature in which there was a cause of fear or sorrow. So the necessity of fear and the nature of pain were not in him as in us.
claims: Hilary means Christ had no cause or merit of pain in himself.
Passion had no dominion over Christ.
Christ had no necessity of fear as we do.

pl-l3d15c3.summary: Addresses obscure chapters of Hilary that seem to deny Christ felt pain. Hilary says blows and wounds fell on Christ like a weapon passing through water, fire, or air, bringing the force of suffering without its pain, since Christ's body, which walked on water and passed through closed doors, did not have the nature to feel pain; he did not fear the nails who restored an ear by a touch. Lombard reads Hilary as meaning that Christ's body felt the force of suffering without its sense in that he had in himself no cause or merit of pain: his flesh did not have our nature of pain, passion had no dominion over him, and the necessity of fear and the nature of pain were not in him as in us.
claims: Hilary seems to deny that Christ felt pain.
Hilary means Christ had no cause or merit of pain in himself.
Passion had no dominion over Christ.
Christ had no necessity of fear or nature of pain as we do.
